group.line: A declarative manifest runtime, a capability probe that picks the cheapest freshness path, a hierarchical token bucket, an MCP client and a hashing normaliser carry every app into one shape.
group.dumb: Each company app is connected by a short form, and a probe learns what that app can do. A budget keeps us inside each app's limits. Apps that already speak the shared AI tool language are called live. Whatever we read is rewritten into a small card with a fixed address and a fingerprint, and the apps stay the owners of the real content.

so_sdk.line:
Declarative connector manifest plus a sandboxed code hook (low-code, as in Airbyte)
requests = ceil(changed / page_size) + 1
so_sdk.dumb: A new app joins by filling in a form, not by writing a program. The form says how to sign in, which lists to read, how paging works and where the 'changed since' marker lives. Only odd apps need a small piece of code, and that code runs in a locked box.
so_sdk.inn: Manifest {app, version, auth{type, authorize_url, token_url, scopes[]}, streams[{name, path, paginator, cursor_field, record_selector, acl_mapping}], hooks{}}; token from so_oauth or so_svc; budget grants from so_rate.
so_sdk.out: Raw app records with their cursor position {stream, records[], next_cursor, acl_raw} sent to so_apps calls and then to so_norm; a descriptor request to so_cap.
so_sdk.store: Reads manifests from the connector registry (versioned, signed). Writes nothing of its own; cursors go to ch_cursor, records go to so_norm in memory only.
so_sdk.fail: Manifest fails schema validation: the connector refuses to load, 0 calls made, the author sees the failing path. Call returns 5xx: 3 attempts at 1 s, 4 s and 16 s, then the page is parked in the dead-letter queue (ch_dlq) with its cursor. A hook crashes or runs over 30 s: it is killed, the page is parked, and the stream continues.
so_sdk.hard: Which share of the top 50 apps can be pure manifest, with no code hook, is untested.
so_sdk.prop: Proposal: one thin contract per app (auth, streams, paging, cursor, access-list mapping) so adding an app is a mapping file plus auth, as the connector sources describe.

deep.purpose: Define every connector as data the runtime interprets, with a small sandboxed hook for the cases data cannot express.
expected: A valid manifest runs a full list and read with no custom code
The cursor returned by one page is exactly the cursor sent on the next call
A manifest change is versioned and takes effect on the next sync, not mid-page
not_expected: It does not choose how often to sync; so_cap and ch_sched do
It does not store document bodies; text passes through memory to so_norm and the transient path

algorithm.name: Manifest interpreter with a code escape hatch
algorithm.formula: pages = ceil(changed / page_size) + 1 (the +1 confirms the end);  cursor_next = record_selector(response).cursor_field
steps: Validate the manifest against the schema and the host allowlist for the app
Resolve auth from the vault by (tenant, app) and ask so_rate for a budget grant
Call the stream path with page_size and cursor, following the paginator type (cursor, offset or link)
Run the record selector and acl_mapping; call a hook only if the manifest names one, inside the sandbox
Return records and next_cursor; persist the cursor only after the batch commits downstream

params.host_allowlist: only the app's registered API hosts

definitions: changed: records changed since the cursor
requests: calls for one incremental pass
math.derivation: Each page returns page_size records and the last call returns a short or empty page, so a pass needs the ceiling plus one confirming call.
math.worked_example: changed = 1,250 records, page_size = 100: ceil(1250/100) = 13, plus 1 = 14 calls. A full sync of N = 2,000,000 at the same page size would need 20,001 calls, which is why incremental cursors matter.
failure_modes: A vendor that ignores page_size returns oversized pages: the paginator caps records per page in memory
Cursor field absent on some records: the stream falls back to full list and flags it in the descriptor
math.calibration: Set page_size to the vendor maximum unless response time exceeds 5 s; then halve it.

alternatives.name: Write each connector in code
alternatives.why_rejected: Every app is a snowflake (t_t49) but most differences are data; code per app costs more to review and secure.

alternatives.name: Only manifests, no hook
alternatives.why_rejected: Some apps need signing or odd paging; without a hook those apps could not join.

security: Tool poisoning through a manifest: a manifest with a redirect or extra host could leak tokens. Control: calls are limited to the host allowlist, redirects off the allowlist are refused, and manifests are signed and reviewed
A hook reading secrets or calling out: control is a sandbox with no network except the app host and no direct vault access, only a scoped token handle
Injection through record content: fields from the app are treated as data and never evaluated or used to build a URL
Cross-tenant read: every call carries the tenant's own token, and a connector instance is bound to one tenant

performance.slo: p95 under 1 s overhead per page beyond the vendor's response time (design)
performance.scaling: At 10x apps the cost is manifest review, not compute; the registry caches parsed manifests and runs one worker pool per (tenant, app).

edge_cases: Empty stream: 1 call, 0 records, cursor unchanged
Huge page: records capped in memory and the rest streamed
Duplicate record across pages: passed on, deduped by ch_dedupe
Concurrent syncs for one stream: per (tenant, app, stream) lock
Unicode in field names: kept as-is, mapped through the manifest
A new app joins by writing a manifest; if it ships an MCP server, so_mcp covers live read with no manifest at all

tests.name: pagination
tests.expect: 14 calls, cursor from page 13 saved only after commit

tests.name: host allowlist
tests.expect: request refused, 1 alert

tests.name: bad manifest
tests.expect: load fails naming both paths, 0 calls

tests.name: hook timeout
tests.expect: hook killed at 30 s, page parked in dead-letter queue

cost_levers: Vendor maximum page size and incremental cursors keep call counts low
feedback_events: Connector author marks a failing stream; admin reports missing records

papers.key_idea: Connectors need a least-privilege review before joining.
papers.how: Manifest scopes are checked against the catalog before a connector loads.

repos.name: Airbyte
repos.take: Low-code connector manifests with streams, pagination and incremental cursors.

repos.name: Nango
repos.take: Sync scripts that emit only metadata if configured; relevant to pointer-only sync.

repos.name: dlt
repos.take: Light connectors that record metadata and cursors.

deep.industry: Glean connectors fetch, map to a common document and push (t_t47); Microsoft ships prebuilt connectors plus a schema SDK for the long tail (t_t50).

so_sdk.req: Requirement: 'Read and write every tool the company uses through APIs'

so_cap.line:
Capability descriptor {webhook, delta, list, search, acl_api, rate}; pick the cheapest path that meets lag
cost(path) = calls per hour
so_cap.dumb: Every app can tell us different things: some push a ping when something changes, some keep a 'changed since' list, some only let us list everything. We ask each app once and write down what it can do. Then we pick the cheapest way that still keeps the brain fresh enough.
so_cap.inn: Probe results {app, endpoint, status, headers}; freshness target per tenant and app {target_lag_s}; vendor terms flags {store_allowed} from gv_tos.
so_cap.out: Capability descriptor {app, webhook: bool, delta: bool, list: bool, search: bool, acl_api: bool, rate: {limit, window_s}, store_allowed: bool, max_webhook_latency_s}; chosen path {primary, backstop, sweep_interval_s}.
so_cap.store: Reads probe responses and gv_tos flags. Writes one descriptor per (tenant, app) to the connector registry, re-probed weekly.
so_cap.fail: Probe call fails: 3 attempts at 1 s, 4 s and 16 s, then the descriptor keeps its last good values and is marked stale; after 14 days stale, the lag monitor alerts. Contradictory results (say webhook works but never fires in 24 h): the path falls back to polling and the descriptor flags webhook_unreliable.
so_cap.hard: How to detect a vendor that quietly changes its delta behaviour between weekly probes is open.
so_cap.prop: Proposal: freshness methods differ per vendor, and sources report no delta API for Notion, Jira, GitHub, HubSpot, Linear or Figma, so the choice of path must be data, not code.

deep.purpose: Record what each app can do and choose the cheapest freshness path that still meets the tenant's lag target.
expected: An app with webhook and delta gets webhook as doorbell, delta as the read, and a polling backstop
An app with no delta gets list polling plus the reconciliation sweep
An app with store_allowed false gets live query only and no content index path
not_expected: It does not run the sync; ch_sched and ch_wf do
It does not change vendor terms; gv_tos owns them

algorithm.name: Constraint-based path selection over a capability descriptor
algorithm.formula: choose argmin over paths of cost(path) = calls_per_hour(path)  subject to lag(path) <= target_lag
steps: Probe: list, webhook registration, delta cursor start, search and access-list endpoints, and read rate-limit headers
Build the descriptor and mark unknown fields false until proven
Enumerate legal paths: webhook+delta, delta poll, list poll; each adds a sweep
Compute lag(path): webhook path is bounded by the vendor's maximum delivery latency unless a backstop poll is added; poll path is interval plus p99 fetch time
Pick the cheapest path that meets target_lag, add the backstop and sweep interval, and write the choice

params.target_lag: 15 minutes (default, tune per tenant by asking what staleness hurts)
params.sweep_interval: 7 days (default, from the reconciliation scan in the research)

math.formula_full: lag(webhook only) = L_webhook;  lag(poll) = I + F;  require lag <= target
math.derivation: A webhook alone is only as good as its worst delivery, so webhook paths need a backstop poll sized to the target. Polling lag is the interval plus one fetch.
math.worked_example: Graph driveItem notifications have an average under 1 minute but a maximum of 6 hours (t_t01). With target = 900 s, webhook alone gives up to 21,600 s, which fails. A backstop poll with I = 840 s and F = 40 s gives 880 s, which passes. Cost: 3600/840 = 4.3 polls per hour per stream.
math.complexity: O(paths), a handful; run once per probe.
failure_modes: A vendor with no delta (Notion, Jira, GitHub, HubSpot, Linear, Figma in our research) forces list polling, whose cost grows with N: the sweep and poll cover it, and the descriptor sets expected_lag higher
Webhook subscription expires (Graph driveItem up to 42,300 minutes, t_t01): the descriptor stores expiry so the scheduler renews early
math.calibration: Set target per tenant from a question to the admin: how stale may an answer be. Check the real lag from the freshness monitor weekly and tighten or loosen.

alternatives.name: Hard-code a path per app
alternatives.why_rejected: Vendors change; a data descriptor can be corrected without a release.

alternatives.name: Always webhook
alternatives.why_rejected: Messages are lost and delayed (t_t54); a backstop is required.

security: Spoofed webhook: a descriptor that says webhook works could be fed by a forged sender. Control: the descriptor records only that the vendor accepted our registration and the receiver verifies each signature elsewhere (ch_hook)
Descriptor poisoning by a tenant admin: control is that only the probe writes descriptor fields, never a manual edit without audit
Probe costing the tenant quota: probes use 1 to 3 calls each and go through so_rate
Terms bypass: store_allowed from gv_tos cannot be overridden by a probe

performance.slo: p95 probe set under 10 s per app (design); runs weekly, off the query path
performance.scaling: At 10x apps probes are 10x calls per week, still negligible; run them in a fair queue.

edge_cases: App unreachable during probe: stale descriptor kept
Tenant with a private instance (custom domain): probe uses the tenant's base URL
Vendor lists webhook support but our plan does not include it: registration fails, descriptor says false
Concurrent probes for one app: single flight
Clock skew in expiry fields: renew when 20 percent of lifetime remains
A new app joins by manifest (so_sdk) or MCP bridge (so_mcp); its first probe fills the descriptor and nothing else needs code

tests.name: backstop sized
tests.given: target 900 s, webhook max latency 21,600 s
tests.expect: descriptor adds poll with interval at most 860 s

tests.name: no delta
tests.expect: path list poll plus sweep, delta false

tests.name: store flag
tests.given: gv_tos says store_allowed false for Slack
tests.expect: descriptor path is live only

tests.name: stale probe
tests.expect: last good descriptor kept, marked stale

cost_levers: Probe weekly and cache results; poll only when the descriptor demands it
feedback_events: Operator marks a path wrong when lag alarms; this retriggers a probe

papers.key_idea: Stale index entries can be worse than none.
papers.how: The backstop and lag target stop silent staleness.

repos.name: Pipedream
repos.take: Open registry of webhook and polling triggers per app, a model for the descriptor values.

repos.name: CocoIndex
repos.take: Change detection and lineage as core features.

deep.industry: Microsoft pairs webhooks with delta queries and renewal jobs (t_t01, t_t02); Google treats push as a doorbell and re-reads the changes list (t_t03).

so_cap.req: Requirement: 'Read and write every tool the company uses through APIs'

so_rate.line:
Hierarchical token bucket per (tenant, app, endpoint); honours Retry-After; fair queue across tenants
tokens = min(B, tokens + r * dt)
so_rate.dumb: Every app only lets us make so many requests per hour. We keep a budget for each company and each app and each kind of call, and we hand out a ticket before every request. If the app says 'slow down', we stop that budget until it says we can go again, and one company never uses up another's share.
so_rate.inn: Budget request {tenant_id, app_id, endpoint, cost, priority: live|backfill}; vendor feedback {status: 429, retry_after_s, remaining, reset_at}.
so_rate.out: Grant {tenant_id, app_id, endpoint, tokens, wait_ms} or deny {reason: paused|empty, retry_after_ms}.
so_rate.store: State in memory with a periodic checkpoint every 10 s to a shared store, keyed (tenant, app, endpoint). Reads quota settings from the capability descriptor. Writes no document data.
so_rate.fail: Shared store unreachable: each worker keeps its last known bucket and refills at 50 percent of the nominal rate for up to 60 s, then pauses and pages the on-call. A 429 without Retry-After: backoff 1 s, 2 s, 4 s up to 60 s with full jitter. Clock jump: refill uses monotonic time only.
so_rate.hard: Fair weighting for tenants of different size, and how to split a quota the vendor shares across several of our connections, is open.
so_rate.prop: Proposal: each vendor sets its own limits (hourly points, per-second bursts, tight per-minute caps), so quota must be modelled per tenant, app and endpoint with a reserved share for live traffic.

deep.purpose: Keep every call inside the vendor's quota, protect live traffic from backfill, and stop one tenant from starving another.
expected: A tenant's backfill never takes more than its configured share of the hourly quota
After a 429 with Retry-After, no call to that bucket is made before the stated time
Two tenants with full queues each get service in proportion to their weights
not_expected: It does not decide what to fetch; callers do
It does not retry calls; it only grants or delays them

algorithm.name: Hierarchical token bucket with deficit round robin
algorithm.formula: tokens(t) = min(B, tokens(t0) + r * (t - t0));  grant iff child.tokens >= cost AND parent.tokens >= cost
steps: Refill each bucket by r times elapsed time, capped at burst B, using a monotonic clock
On a request, check the endpoint bucket then the (tenant, app) parent bucket; both must hold the cost
Live requests may use up to 100 percent; backfill may use at most its share (default 50 percent) of the parent
If empty, queue the request; tenants are served by deficit round robin so each gets quantum proportional to its weight
On a 429, set the bucket paused until now + Retry-After and drop its tokens to 0

params.backfill_share: 50 percent (estimate from t_t06, tune per tenant)
params.burst_B: vendor's per-second burst cap, for example 100 requests per second for Jira GET (t_t06)

definitions: r: refill rate in tokens per second
cost: tokens for one call (some vendors price calls in points)
math.formula_full: r = Q / 3600;  backfill_rate = s * r;  live_reserved = (1 - s) * r
math.derivation: A bucket that refills at the quota rate never lets average use exceed the quota, and the burst cap B limits short spikes to what the vendor allows.
math.worked_example: Jira standard tenant: quota = 100,000 + 10 * users points per hour, capped at 500,000 (t_t06). For 200 users: Q = 102,000, r = 28.3 points/s. Backfill share 50 percent: 51,000 points/hour. Identity reads cost 2 points per object (t_t06), so backfill can fetch 25,500 identity objects per hour. Slack non-marketplace: conversations.history is 1 request/min with 15 objects per page (t_t07), which is why Slack is live only. Notion: about 3 requests/s per connection (t_t08).
math.complexity: O(1) per grant; DRR adds O(number of active tenants) per scheduling round.
failure_modes: Quota overrun blocks until the next UTC hour for Jira (t_t06): the budgeter keeps a reserve to avoid it
Hours-long windows (t_t09): reserve a slice for freshness traffic so live sync survives a drained quota
math.calibration: Start backfill share at 50 percent, then raise it only when the freshness monitor shows live lag below half its target for 7 days.

alternatives.name: One global limiter
alternatives.why_rejected: A noisy tenant or app would block the rest; limits differ per app and endpoint (t_t48).

alternatives.name: Retry on 429 without a budget
alternatives.why_rejected: Retries add load exactly when the vendor is saying stop.

security: Noisy neighbour: one tenant floods a shared limiter. Control: per-tenant buckets and deficit round robin so each tenant gets only its weighted share
Quota exhaustion as a denial of service on live traffic by our own backfill. Control: a reserved live share (default 50 percent)
Forged vendor feedback (a spoofed Retry-After from a bad proxy): control is that feedback is read only from the TLS response of the vendor host
Budget request flood from a buggy connector: per-caller cap on queued requests, 1,000 by default (design), then reject

performance.slo: p95 grant under 2 ms in process (design)
performance.scaling: At 10x tenants the shared checkpoint store becomes the limit; shard the buckets by tenant hash and keep the hot state in process.

edge_cases: Empty quota: request queued, not dropped, up to 10 minutes then returned as deny
Huge cost (a single call costing more than B): rejected with a clear error
Same request granted twice by two workers after failover: the vendor 429 and the bucket pause correct it within one window
Concurrent grants on one bucket: atomic decrement
Clock skew: monotonic clock only; wall time used for Retry-After conversions
MCP calls from so_mcp share the same bucket as native calls, so a new app joining by manifest or MCP gets the same protection

tests.name: retry-after
tests.expect: no grant for that bucket for 30 s

tests.name: backfill share
tests.expect: backfill capped at 51,000 points per hour

tests.name: fair queue
tests.given: tenants A and B weight 1 each, both backlogged
tests.expect: grants alternate 1:1

tests.name: burst cap
tests.expect: 100 granted at once, rest paced at r

cost_levers: Larger backfill share finishes onboarding sooner but costs live freshness; tune per tenant
feedback_events: Operator overrides a share after a freshness alarm; vendor 429 counts feed tuning

papers.key_idea: Use the failure points as a test checklist.
papers.how: Quota exhaustion maps to its failure points around missing content and incomplete answers.

repos.name: Temporal
repos.take: Durable retries and long waits for jobs that sleep until a quota window reopens.

deep.industry: Dash and Glean run per-connector queues because limits differ (t_t48); Atlassian, Notion and Slack publish the limits we model (t_t06, t_t08, t_t07).

so_rate.req: Requirement: 'Read and write every tool the company uses through APIs'

so_mcp.line:
MCP client with audience-bound tokens, pinned tool list, read tools only
P(some source times out) = 1 - (1 - p)^n
so_mcp.dumb: Some apps already offer their own search and read tools that any AI helper can call. The MCP bridge calls those tools for the asking person, using that person's own key. It lets us add such an app without building a custom connector.
so_mcp.inn: Tool call {tenant_id, user_id, app_id, tool, arguments, deadline_ms}; per-user token from so_obo; budget grant from so_rate.
so_mcp.out: Tool result {app_id, tool, items[{native_id, title, snippet, url, modified_at}], truncated, ms} or an error {code: timeout|denied|upstream_down}. Items go to so_norm.
so_mcp.store: Reads the pinned tool list per (app, server version) from the registry. Writes nothing; results stay in memory for the request. Writes an audit row per call to pl_idp.
so_mcp.fail: Server timeout at the call deadline (default 3 s): the source is dropped, the answer says it was skipped, no retry on the query path. Server returns an error: 1 retry after 200 ms only for read tools, then drop. Tool list differs from the pinned hash: the bridge refuses to call and alerts an admin.
so_mcp.hard: Dash reports simple MCP queries taking up to 45 s (t_t11), so whether a 3 s budget leaves useful results for slow servers is open.
so_mcp.prop: Proposal: any app that ships an MCP server becomes a live-read path without a custom crawler (t_t51), but tokens must be audience-bound and never passed through (t_t24).

deep.purpose: Call an app's own MCP server for live read and search, as the asking user, when no native connector exists or the app forbids copies.
expected: Only tools on the allowlist (read and search) are callable
Each call carries a token whose audience is that server
A slow server delays the answer by no more than the deadline
not_expected: It does not index what it fetches; results are not stored
It does not call write tools; ll_ro and the policy layer own actions

algorithm.name: MCP client with pinned tools and deadline budget
algorithm.formula: P(at least one of n sources times out) = 1 - (1 - p)^n;  per-source deadline = min(3 s, remaining_budget)
steps: Look up the server and its pinned tool list hash; fetch the live list and compare
Ask so_obo for a token with resource set to the server (RFC 8707)
Ask so_rate for a budget grant, then call the allowed tool with the deadline
Validate result shape; truncate to 10 items; pass to so_norm
Write the audit row; on timeout or error return a typed error, never partial text as a success

definitions: p: probability one source times out
P: chance at least one times out
math.derivation: Calls run in parallel; the answer is complete only if every call returns, so the chance of a gap grows with n.
math.worked_example: p = 0.05, n = 4: P = 1 - 0.95^4 = 1 - 0.8145 = 0.1855, so about 1 in 5 live answers is missing a source. With a 3 s deadline the answer is still returned and says which source was skipped.
math.complexity: O(n) calls in parallel; latency is the slowest source up to the deadline.
failure_modes: Slow tools make the deadline the dominant cost: sources are ranked by their recent p95 and the router prunes slow ones
Tool descriptions eat context (t_t19): expose one search tool per server to the planner, not all of them
math.calibration: Set deadline at the p90 of recent latency per server, never above 3 s on the query path; review monthly.

alternatives.name: Native crawler per app
alternatives.why_rejected: Costly for the long tail; MCP covers apps that ship a server (t_t51).

alternatives.name: Pass the client's token to the server
alternatives.why_rejected: Banned by the MCP authorization rules (t_t24).

security: Tool poisoning: a server changes a tool description to steer the model. Control: the tool list is pinned by hash, changes need admin approval, and descriptions never reach the model unreviewed
Indirect injection through results (t_t52): control is that every item goes to qr_inj as untrusted data and carries no instructions
Token passthrough and confused deputy: control is per-user audience-bound tokens from so_obo (t_t24)
SSRF through a server URL: only registered server URLs are callable, and redirects off them are refused
Server returns more than asked (data exfil): result size capped at 10 items and 4 KB per snippet

performance.scaling: At 10x queries the limit is each vendor's tool limits (for Slack MCP Tier 2 about 20+ per minute, t_t25); so_rate shares them and the router prefers the index for common queries.

edge_cases: Server returns empty: valid answer, recorded as no hits
Huge result: truncated at 10 items with truncated true
Duplicate item in two servers: deduped by URI downstream
Server down: breaker after 5 failures in 30 s, source skipped for 60 s
Unicode in snippets: passed through as text, never executed
A new app joins through the MCP bridge by registering its server URL, pinning its tool list and approving scopes; no connector code is written

tests.name: pinned tools
tests.expect: call refused, admin alert, 0 results

tests.name: deadline
tests.expect: dropped at 3 s, answer notes the skipped source

tests.name: audience
tests.given: token for app A sent to server B
tests.expect: server B rejects, bridge audits

tests.name: write tool
tests.given: planner asks for a create tool
tests.expect: denied, not on allowlist

cost_levers: Parallel calls with a 3 s deadline; cache nothing; prefer the index for common queries
feedback_events: User marks a missing live source; admin reviews skipped-source counts

analytics_events.name: mcp.pin_mismatch
analytics_events.when: when a tool list differs from its pin

papers.key_idea: MCP threat model: scoped tokens, tool allowlists, audit.
papers.how: Pinned tool list, allowlist and audit rows adopt it directly.
Each server is reviewed before it is registered.

repos.name: MCP reference servers
repos.take: Pattern for exposing an app as live tools.

repos.name: agentgateway
repos.take: Proxy where tool allow-lists and per-user tokens can be enforced.

deep.industry: Slack's MCP server uses user tokens, per-tool scopes and admin approval (t_t25) and went generally available on 2026-02-17 (t_t13); Microsoft uses federated connectors over MCP for sensitive sources (t_t12).

so_mcp.req: Requirement: 'Read and write every tool the company uses through APIs'

so_norm.line:
Envelope {uri, version, content_hash, acl_ref} with SHA-256 over canonical content
P(collision) = n^2 / 2^(b+1)
so_norm.dumb: Every app describes a document in its own way. We rewrite each one into the same small card with a fixed address, a version number and a fingerprint of its contents. The fingerprint lets us skip anything that has not truly changed, and the card never carries the full text.
so_norm.inn: Raw app object {native_id, kind-specific fields, modified_at, sharing fields} from so_apps; manifest mapping from so_sdk; tenant and app ids.
so_norm.out: Envelope {uri, app, tenant, kind: Document|Message|Principal|Event, version, content_hash, modified_at, acl_ref, title, container, author} sent to ch_bus; text handed in memory to the transient path, never persisted by this component.
so_norm.store: Reads mapping rules from the connector registry. Writes nothing durable: the envelope goes to the change event log (ch_bus). Message bodies from sources with store_allowed false are dropped after hashing, or not fetched at all.
so_norm.fail: Unmapped required field: the record is rejected with the field path and parked in the dead-letter queue after 0 retries (a retry cannot fix it), and the stream continues. Hash computation error: 1 retry, then park. More than 5 percent of a batch rejected in 10 minutes: the stream pauses and alerts.
so_norm.hard: The exact list of fields included in the canonical form for each app, so view counts or timestamps do not cause false changes, must be tuned per app.
so_norm.prop: Proposal: the brain needs one thin shape for every app (id, access list reference, text pointer, timestamps, type), as Dropbox describes, so downstream stages stay app-agnostic.

deep.purpose: Turn each app object into one of four envelopes with a stable address, a version and a content hash, so change detection and deduplication work the same for every app.
expected: The same object always gets the same uri and, if unchanged, the same content_hash
A change to a volatile field (view count) does not change the hash
not_expected: It does not decide whether the person may see the object; acl_ref points to the access list
It does not extract text; the transient path does

algorithm.name: Canonicalise then hash
algorithm.formula: content_hash = SHA-256(canonical(selected fields));  uri = devx://{tenant}/{app}/{kind}/{native_id};  version = vendor revision else modified_at
steps: Pick the fields per kind from the mapping; drop volatile fields (counts, last viewed)
Canonicalise: sort keys, Unicode NFC, trim whitespace, fixed number formatting
Hash with SHA-256 and hex-encode
Build the uri from tenant, app, kind and native id, escaping reserved characters
Set version from the vendor's revision or etag; if none, use modified_at and break ties by hash; emit the envelope

definitions: P: probability of any collision (birthday bound)
math.derivation: With n items and b bits, there are about n^2/2 pairs, each colliding with probability 2^-b.
math.worked_example: n = 10^9 documents. With a 64-bit hash (Notion uses a 64-bit hash per span, t_t44): P = 10^18 / 2^65 = 10^18 / 3.69e19 = 0.027, about 2.7 percent, too high for whole-document identity. With SHA-256, b = 256: P = 10^18 / 2^257 = 10^18 / 2.3e77, about 4e-60.
math.complexity: O(size of selected fields) per object; under 1 ms for typical documents.
failure_modes: Hash of unnormalised text flips on whitespace: canonicalisation removes it
Two different documents with the same native_id across apps: the uri includes app and tenant
math.calibration: Use 256 bits at document level; chunk-level hashes downstream may use 64 bits because n per document is small.

alternatives.name: Store raw vendor JSON
alternatives.why_rejected: Copies the content and ties every downstream stage to each vendor's shape.

alternatives.name: Hash only modified_at
alternatives.why_rejected: Edits that do not move modified_at, and touches that do not change content, both go wrong.

security: Poisoned content (p_poisoned-rag): the author field and source are recorded so trust can be applied later; control is that the envelope carries author and container id, not text
Collision attack where an attacker crafts two documents with equal hashes: control is a collision-resistant hash (SHA-256)
Injection via metadata (title with instructions): control is that metadata is data and is passed to qr_inj when shown to a model
Cross-tenant envelope: uri contains the tenant id and the bus rejects an envelope whose tenant differs from its connector's

performance.scaling: At 10x volume it scales linearly with workers; the cost is CPU for hashing, trivial against vendor calls.

edge_cases: Empty body: hash of empty canonical form, valid
Huge object (100 MB file): only metadata hashed here; the body hash is taken by the transient path while streaming
Duplicate event for the same version: same envelope, deduped by ch_dedupe
Concurrent updates: version breaks ties
Unicode in title: NFC
Clock skew in modified_at: version uses the vendor revision when it exists
A new app joins by mapping fields into the four envelopes in its manifest (so_sdk) or the MCP bridge result shape (so_mcp)

so_apps.line:
Vendor REST, GraphQL and webhook APIs; the system of record stays here
staleness bound = min(webhook max latency, poll interval + p99 fetch)
so_apps.dumb: These are the company's real tools, like Slack, Drive, Microsoft 365, Notion, Jira, GitHub and the customer database. They keep the truth. The brain only asks them questions and remembers where things are.
so_apps.inn: Authenticated HTTPS requests {method, path, cursor, page_size} or MCP tool calls; webhook registrations {callback_url, secret, event types}.
so_apps.out: JSON responses with app-native ids, times and sharing fields; webhook posts that carry little or no content (Google push has an empty body, t_t03); rate-limit headers.
so_apps.store: Owns all source content and permissions. The brain stores none of it here; whatever the brain keeps is derived and listed in the index stage.
so_apps.fail: The app returns 429: so_rate pauses that bucket for Retry-After. App returns 5xx: 3 attempts at 1 s, 4 s and 16 s, then the page is parked. App outage over 24 h: the lag monitor reports it and answers mark the source stale. Slack stays live only, so a Slack outage means an honest 'source unavailable' answer.
so_apps.hard: No research source covers delta APIs for Notion, Jira, GitHub, HubSpot, Linear or Figma; our design covers them with polling and the reconciliation sweep.
so_apps.prop: Proposal: the system of record stays in each app so the brain never becomes a second source of truth; Slack's API terms bar persistent copies and indexes of its search data, so Slack is queried live.

deep.purpose: Name and bound what we rely on in each app: change signals, limits and terms, so the rest of the design can plan for the worst case rather than the average.
expected: Each app is read with the least access that works
Vendor limits are respected through so_rate
Terms that bar copying (Slack) switch the app to live query only
not_expected: It does not belong to the brain; the brain cannot assume uptime or schema stability
It does not guarantee delivery of any change notification

algorithm.name: Vendor contract table
algorithm.formula: staleness_bound = min(L_max, I + F), where L_max is the vendor's worst delivery latency, I the poll interval, F the p99 fetch time
steps: Record, per vendor, the change signal (webhook, delta, none), its expiry, and its limits from the research
Mark vendors with copy bans as live only
Plan the backstop poll and sweep from the worst delivery latency, not the average
Re-check the table at every capability probe
Escalate when a vendor changes terms (gv_tos)

params.notion: about 3 requests per second per connection (t_t08)
params.slack_history: 1 request per minute, 15 objects per page for non-Marketplace apps (t_t07)

definitions: L_max: vendor worst-case webhook delivery latency
math.derivation: A backstop poll caps staleness at one interval plus one fetch, whatever the webhook does.
math.worked_example: driveItem L_max = 21,600 s (6 h, t_t01). Poll I = 840 s, F = 40 s: bound = min(21,600, 880) = 880 s, about 14.7 minutes.
failure_modes: Vendor silently changes limits: the capability probe re-reads headers weekly
A vendor adds a delta API later: the descriptor can switch paths without a release
math.calibration: Review the table each quarter against vendor docs; record the date of each fact.

alternatives.name: Copy everything into the brain
alternatives.why_rejected: Violates Slack terms (t_t07, t_t13) and makes the brain a second source of truth.

security: A forged webhook from a spoofed sender: control is a shared secret or signature check at ch_hook before enqueueing
Overbroad token at the vendor: control is read-only catalog scopes and a 180 day review
Prompt injection planted in an app document by any writer (p_poisoned-rag): control is that all fetched content is untrusted data (qr_inj)
Vendor-side breach: tokens are short-lived and wrapped per tenant; revocation is one call per connection

performance.slo: p95 vendor latency varies; the brain's budget is a 3 s deadline on the query path (design)
performance.scaling: At 10x load the vendor limit is the bound; so_rate shares it and the router prefers the index.

edge_cases: Vendor outage: answers mark the source stale or unavailable
Vendor changes a field name: the schema normaliser rejects records and alerts
Vendor deletes data: delete events become tombstones; the sweep finds those missed
Rate limit window long (hours): reserve a freshness slice (t_t09)
Unicode: kept as-is
A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) if it has a REST API, or the MCP bridge (so_mcp) if it ships an MCP server

tests.expect: no content stored; live path used

tests.expect: poll catches the change within 880 s

tests.expect: renewed with overlap before expiry

cost_levers: Vendor tier and quota are the main cost; prefer webhooks plus delta over frequent full polls
feedback_events: Admins report stale or missing items; the lag monitor attributes them to a vendor

papers.key_idea: Stale entries can be worse than none.
papers.how: Bounding staleness per vendor feeds the freshness stamp.

edges.d: Records {stream, native_id, fields, modified_at, acl_raw} for envelope building
Cursor {tenant_id, app_id, stream, cursor} written only after the batch commits
Failed page {stream, cursor, error, attempts: 3} for later replay
Capability descriptor {webhook, delta, list, acl_api, store_allowed} that selects streams to run
Descriptor flag and subscription expiry {app, webhook, expires_at} so the receiver registers and renews
Descriptor flag {app, delta, cursor_kind} telling the poller whether a cursor exists
Backfill budget {tenant, app, tokens_per_hour} capped at its share of quota
Pause {tenant, app, endpoint, retry_after_s} so durable workflows sleep rather than retry
Items {native_id, title, snippet, url, modified_at} normalised for the live path
Live search items with url and version for hydration and ranking
Audit row {tenant_id, user_id, app_id, tool, outcome}
uri, version, content_hash, modified_at, acl_ref to be stored as the pointer record
Headers {status 429, Retry-After, remaining, reset_at} returned to the budgeter
Webhook {event_type, resource id, signature}; often no content, only a doorbell
Admin consent or install grant {tenant_id, app_id, scopes[], granted_by} returned by the app's consent screen
Responses to the capability probe {endpoint, status, headers}
